text:
B: Hello. Can you hear me?
A: Yes, hello. I'm Kasia.
B: Kulwinder. Hello.
A: Hello. How are you finding it so far?
B: It's alright. I keep wondering what they're actually looking at. Whether we get on, or how we talk, or what.
A: I wondered that also. I think maybe just if strangers can talk for three minutes without it being awkward.
B: Well, we'll see. Where are you?
A: Warrington. I'm from Poland originally, but I've been here a long time. You?
B: Hayes, West London. Born there, never really left.
A: Do you work, or...?
B: Not now. I was a tailor. Alterations. My hands went, arthritis, so I stopped. You?
A: I'm a biomedical scientist, in a hospital lab. Haematology, so I look at blood all day.
B: Everyone's in hospitals today. I just had a nurse. Can I ask you something, then, since you're blood?
A: Of course. But I'm not a doctor, I should say.
B: No, it's my mum. She's got blood pressure tablets and she won't take them properly. She says she feels fine, so why take them. She takes one, skips two days. Does that matter, or am I going on at her for nothing?
A: Erm. Honestly, it matters, yes. Blood pressure you usually don't feel, that's the problem. Feeling fine doesn't mean it's fine. But I'm not the right person for her dose. Her GP or the pharmacist, they can maybe give her the pill box with the days on it. My mum has one in Poland, and my brother checks it.
B: She'd hate a pill box. She'd say it's for old people. She's eighty-one.
A: Ha. Mine is seventy-four and says exactly the same.
B: They're all the same, mums. Is your mum still over there, then?
A: Yes, in Opole. She phones every Sunday evening. I go once or twice a year. It's... not enough, sometimes. But it's what it is.
B: Mm. Mine's ten minutes away and comes round every day, so I've got the other problem.
A: Maybe we should swap for a week.
B: You can have her. She'll reorganise your kitchen.
A: My kitchen needs it, honestly. Do you cook a lot?
B: Every night. Dinner from scratch. Dal, sabzi, rotis. I batch-cook Sundays.
A: I cook most nights also, for tea. My husband's family say tea, so now I say it. My mum thinks it's crazy, a meal called after a drink. At Christmas I make pierogi, hundreds of them, from my grandmother's recipe, and I don't measure anything, I just do it by how the dough feels. My husband tried once and they all opened in the water.
B: That's how I do rotis. You can't write it down. My daughter asks how much flour and I say, enough.
A: Enough. Yes, exactly. That's the answer my grandmother gave me.
B: Do you grow anything? I've got chillies and tomatoes in pots.
A: Tomatoes, yes! Mine were terrible this year, the blight came.
B: You have to keep the leaves off the soil. And don't water from the top, water the—
A: Oh, that's the timer.
